title: Vitamin D: Which Foods Have the Most and Why It Is Often Low

seo.title: Vitamin D Foods: Best Sources and Why It Runs Low
seo.meta_description: Fatty fish, UV-exposed mushrooms, and fortified foods are the main dietary sources of vitamin D. Eggs and liver provide smaller amounts. See what matters per serving.
seo.search_intent: Identify the main food sources of vitamin D and explain why dietary intake is often low.

excerpt: Fatty fish are among the few naturally concentrated sources of vitamin D. UV-exposed mushrooms can also provide meaningful amounts, while egg yolk and liver contribute smaller amounts. In the United States, fortified milk and some plant beverages and cereals are important because there are relatively few naturally rich everyday foods.
content_html:
Vitamin D is harder to obtain from food than many other vitamins because only a short list of foods naturally contains much of it. The body can also produce vitamin D in skin exposed to UVB, so dietary intake and vitamin D status are related but not identical questions.

Fatty fish are the strongest everyday natural sources

Salmon, trout, mackerel, herring, and other fatty fish stand out because a normal serving can contribute a large share of the daily target. In the NIH food table, 3 ounces of cooked farmed rainbow trout provide about 16.2 micrograms and 3 ounces of cooked sockeye salmon about 14.2 micrograms. Those figures are useful examples, not fixed values: vitamin D varies with species, origin, farming or wild conditions, and preparation.

Fish-liver oils can be even more concentrated. The same NIH table lists a tablespoon of cod liver oil at 34 micrograms. That does not mean it should be treated as an ordinary cooking oil or taken casually in large amounts; it is a concentrated product with other nutrients as well. For most people looking at foods rather than supplements, fatty fish are the more practical comparison.

Eggs, liver, and mushrooms contribute—but not in the same way

Egg yolk and beef liver contain vitamin D, but generally much less per typical serving than fatty fish. NIH lists a large scrambled egg at about 1.1 micrograms and a 3-ounce serving of braised beef liver at about 1 microgram. They can add to intake, but an egg is not nutritionally equivalent to a serving of salmon for vitamin D.

Mushrooms are different because they mainly provide vitamin D2, and the amount depends heavily on UV exposure. Ordinary mushrooms can contain little, while mushrooms intentionally exposed to ultraviolet light can contain much more. In the NIH table, half a cup of raw sliced UV-exposed white mushrooms provides about 9.2 micrograms. If vitamin D is the reason you are buying them, the label matters because visual appearance alone does not tell you whether they were UV treated.

Fortified foods do much of the work in the United States

Fortification changes the picture considerably. Most U.S. milk is fortified with about 3 micrograms per cup, and many soy, almond, and oat beverages contain similar amounts. Some breakfast cereals, orange juices, yogurts, and margarines are fortified too, but this is product-specific. Cheese and ice cream are not automatically fortified just because they are made from milk.

This is why two otherwise similar breakfasts can differ substantially in vitamin D. A fortified plant beverage can contribute several micrograms while an unfortified version may contribute very little. Checking the Nutrition Facts label is more reliable than assuming that an entire product category is a source.

Why reaching the daily target from food can still be difficult

The U.S. Recommended Dietary Allowance is 15 micrograms (600 IU) per day for most adults through age 70. A serving of a vitamin-D-rich fish can get close to that amount, but a day built around eggs, vegetables, grains, and unfortified foods may provide relatively little. That is why regular use of rich or fortified sources matters much more for vitamin D than simply eating a varied diet.

Vitamin D status also depends on sun exposure, season, latitude, skin pigmentation, age, body and health factors, and individual absorption. A list of foods can explain dietary sources, but it cannot diagnose deficiency or determine an appropriate supplement dose. If a blood test or supplementation is part of the question, that belongs in a clinical discussion rather than being inferred from how much salmon or milk you ate.

faq.question: What food has the most vitamin D?
faq.answer: Fish-liver oils are extremely concentrated, while fatty fish such as trout and salmon are among the strongest practical natural food sources.

faq.question: Do eggs have much vitamin D?
faq.answer: Egg yolks contain vitamin D, but a typical egg provides far less than a serving of fatty fish. NIH lists about 1.1 micrograms for one large scrambled egg.

faq.question: Do mushrooms contain vitamin D?
faq.answer: Some do. UV-exposed mushrooms can contain meaningful vitamin D2, while mushrooms without UV treatment may contain very little. Check the label when vitamin D content matters.

faq.question: Are plant milks a source of vitamin D?
faq.answer: Many U.S. soy, almond, and oat beverages are fortified, often with amounts similar to fortified cow's milk, but not every product is. Check the Nutrition Facts label.
